name: Client Hints: architecture and bitness
plain: CPU family (x86 or ARM) and 32 or 64 bit, via high-entropy Client Hints.
meaning: Reveals Apple Silicon or Windows on ARM vs Intel or AMD, and bitness. Useful to serve the right binary or WebAssembly build; also splits users into hardware cohorts.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can tell if your chip is Intel, AMD, or ARM, and 32 or 64 bit
limits.user_action: Nothing. The site asks and Chromium answers without a prompt
can: See whether you have an Apple Silicon, ARM, Intel, or AMD processor
Check if your system is 32 or 64 bit
Offer the right download or app build
Put you into a hardware group for tracking
cannot: Work in Firefox, Safari, or on iPhone
Get an answer until the site asks for it
See your RAM or disk size
limits.reach_label: Chip family, only when the site asks
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge, and Samsung Internet answer. Firefox and Safari do not.

story.what_it_is: Tells a site whether your chip is ARM or Intel, and whether it is 32 or 64 bit.

marketing.name: User-Agent Client Hints
marketing.pitch: Chrome's replacement for the old user agent string: sites ask for the details they need instead of getting everything.

story.for_you: You never see it. It quietly helps a download page offer the right installer, so you do not get an app that will not run on your Mac. It is the kind of detail that stays out of view.
story.for_makers: Software makers need the right build for each chip. Hardware type also splits people into groups: Apple Silicon owners behave differently from budget Windows machines. Fraud teams compare it against what the user agent claims.

use_cases.example: A download page offers the Apple Silicon version of an app to a Mac with an M-series chip and the Intel version to others.
A web game picks a WebAssembly build tuned for 64 bit memory and threads on a capable machine.
A browser photo editor loads the faster build that uses ARM or SIMD instructions.
An advertiser targets owners of newer Apple Silicon Macs with an offer for pro tools.
A product team counts ARM users to decide whether to ship a separate build.
A fraud tool sees a claimed iPhone user agent with an Intel desktop chip, and flags a fake device.

technical_bounds: Chrome may report empty on some platforms

history.change: Arch and bitness removed from UA string
